fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "A Thalassocracy Built on Receipts", "body": "Chance opens by introducing Dylan's new book, The Real Universal Empire, and the two spend the first stretch on method rather than conclusions. Dylan describes crawling through Godfrey Higgins at a page every thirty or forty minutes, taking notes until scattered dots resolve into a picture, and both hosts insist on receipts: if a claim cannot be looked up, it is probably an error. Chance highlights a word he had to look up from the book, thalassocracy, rule by sea power, and Dylan argues the empire they are tracking was exactly that, colonizing coastlines rather than pushing inland."}, {"title": "The Sanskrit Origin Story Inverted", "body": "Dylan rejects the standard story that Sanskrit and India sit at the headwaters of European language. He asks how the material traveled when India's priestly classes were barred from crossing those borders, and notes that Sanskrit stayed rule bound rather than corrupted by common use. Chance presses the point with a dating rule the two treat as decisive: alphabets gain letters over time and never shed them, so a script with double the letters cannot be the parent. Dylan adds that India's oldest inscriptions run to roughly 250 BC while Italian artifacts are far older, and calls Indo European a language group nobody can actually produce."}, {"title": "The Third Century Forgery Window", "body": "Both hosts argue that the first three centuries of the common era were written backward into place. Dylan points to a marker around 270 AD, roughly when the first Greek writer outside the Jewish mystery schools mentions Moses, and suggests Judea was chosen as the setting precisely because it had no historians, with the Augustan age supplying familiar scenery. Chance credits Reverend Robert Taylor with taking an axe to the whole structure, and Dylan claims the crucified savior already appeared in Italy and Greece long before the Christian era, in artifacts of Ixion that later hands destroyed as supposed Christian forgeries."}, {"title": "Taking Off the Greek Sunglasses", "body": "Dylan quotes the Etruscologist Jocelyn Penny Small, who says that once you take off your Greek sunglasses the Etruscans are simply not Greeks, and stacks up the evidence: ninth century biconical and hut shaped urns, painted tombs the Greeks did not make, and what he calls far more affinity with Egypt than with Greece. Chance raises Etruscan script found on Egyptian sarcophagi, though Dylan cautions the text may be allegorical rather than historical. Both note the freer role of women, the thin line between nobles and serfs, and Godfrey Higgins on feudalism arriving in Europe like an exotic plant."}, {"title": "Two Fathers, No Rome", "body": "The episode closes on the argument its title advertises. Chance says archaeologists never let their findings build the narrative and instead used old accounts, likely Greek and Roman histories introduced to Europe in the Middle Ages, to explain the artifacts in front of them. Dylan cuts in on the two authorities Chance names, Thucydides and Herodotus, the father of history and the father of scientific history, and points out that neither one mentions Rome. Chance is incredulous, saying it would have been the biggest deal, and Dylan adds that Herodotus never mentions Moses either."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: The Real Universal Empire by Dylan Saccoccio traces the origins of Western civilization, written language, and ancient priestcraft back to the seafaring Etruscan culture of pre-Roman Italy rather than to Greece, India, or the Levant. This is the first episode of Inner Whirled, a co-hosted deep-dive series on the book and the research behind it.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: Topics include the Sanskrit and Indo-European origin debate, the oldest evidence of ancient alphabets and why letter count alone exposes the accepted timeline, the cultural affinity between the Etruscans and the Egyptians, why neither Herodotus nor Thucydides ever wrote about Rome, and the strange absence of ancient Italy from mainstream historical writing. This is a remastered episode originally published March 7th 2024.
